claim: The integrated stress response (ISR) is triggered when one of four stress-sensing kinases becomes active: HRI, PKR, PERK, and GCN2.
source: One such pathway, the integrated stress response (ISR), is triggered when one of four stress-sensing kinases becomes active: (1) heme-regulated inhibitor kinase (HRI) is activated by oxidative stress, such as arsenite; (2) protein kinase R (PKR) is activated by viral infections; (3) PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK) is induced when unfolded proteins accumulate (proteotoxic stress) and when the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) becomes stressed; and (4) general control non-depressible 2 (GCN2) is induced in poor nutrient conditions, particularly amino acid deprivation (Costa-Mattioli and Walter, 2020; El-Naggar and Sorensen, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costa-Mattioli and Walter, 2020 and El-Naggar and Sorensen, 2018, which are referenced works in the field.

claim: Activation of any of the four ISR kinases results in phosphorylation of serine 51 of eIF2α.
source: Activation of any of these four kinases results in phosphorylation of serine 51 of eIF2α, a core component of the canonical translational initiation complex.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism in the ISR pathway, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylated eIF2α blocks the guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B from stimulating the eIF2-GTP-methionyl-initiator tRNA ternary complex.
source: Since phosphorated eIF2α blocks the guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B from stimulating the eIF2-GTP-methionyl-initiator tRNA ternary complex, the translation of housekeeping mRNAs is decelerated, and initiation of new protein synthesis is dampened.
evidence: This describes the established molecular mechanism of ISR-mediated translational control.

claim: ISR-competent SCC cells displayed phospho-S51 immunolabeling when treated with sodium arsenite, while eIF2α S51A clones were refractory to phosphorylation.
source: Importantly, when we treated these SCC lines with sodium arsenite to induce oxidative stress and activate the HRI kinase (Sendoel et al., 2017), we observed that like the parental clone, the stressed eIF2α S51 cells displayed phospho-S51 immunolabeling, while the eIF2α S51A clones were refractory to phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and cited work from Sendoel et al., 2017.

claim: All three stressors (sodium arsenite, tunicamycin, and bortezomib) dampened protein synthesis rates in eIF2α S51 SCC cells.
source: Using puromycin incorporation as a gauge to measure nascent protein synthesis, we observed that indeed all three stressors dampened protein synthesis rates in our eIF2α S51 SCC cells (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using puromycin incorporation assays.

claim: Bortezomib inhibited the mTORC1 pathway in both S51 and S51A cells.
source: Suspecting alternative mechanisms, we first showed that bortezomib inhibited the mTORC1 pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mTORC1 is primarily responsible for the global reduction in protein synthesis rates during proteotoxic stress response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon exposure to proteotoxic stress, nearly 3× more eIF2α-S51A cells were positive for the apoptotic marker Annexin-V compared to cells with an intact ISR.
source: However, upon exposure to proteotoxic stress, nearly 3× more eIF2α-S51A cells were positive for the apoptotic marker Annexin-V over counterparts with an intact ISR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pre-oncogenic and fully transformed stem cells were significantly more resistant to bortezomib-induced cell death compared to wild-type stem cells.
source: Interestingly in the presence of bortezomib, pre-oncogenic and fully transformed stem cells were significantly more resistant to cell death compared to wild-type stem cells (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: S51A and S51 SCC cells both formed tumors that grew similarly and showed similar morphologies when injected into immunocompromised mice.
source: Intriguingly, however, when we injected our SCC cells into the skins of immunocompromised, athymic (Nude) mice, S51A and S51 SCC cells both formed tumors that grew similarly and showed similar morphologies (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In vivo S51A SCC tumors exhibited significantly greater sensitivity to proteotoxic stress and apoptosis than their S51 counterparts when treated with bortezomib.
source: Strikingly, and consistent with our in vitro findings, when we treated our mice with bortezomib, the in vivo S51A SCC tumors exhibited significantly greater sensitivity to proteotoxic stress and apoptosis than their counterparts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control SCC cells with a competent ISR recovered and began to proliferate within 24–48 hr after bortezomib pulse, while ISR-null SCC cells took a full 24 hr longer.
source: Following this bortezomib 'pulse,' control SCC cells with a competent ISR recovered and began to proliferate within 24–48 hr. In striking contrast, ISR-null SCC cells took a full 24 hr longer than their counterparts before they began to proliferate again (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The rate at which ubiquitinated proteins were cleared from the insoluble fraction was remarkably reduced in ISR-null cells compared to control SCC cells after withdrawing bortezomib.
source: After withdrawing bortezomib, however, the rate at which ubiquitinated proteins were cleared from the insoluble fraction was remarkably reduced in the ISR-null cells compared to control SCC cell lysates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Inhibiting translation elongation with cyclohexamide or translation initiation with harringtonine almost entirely blocked the buildup of protein aggregates following 6 hr of bortezomib treatment.
source: Inhibiting translation elongation with cyclohexamide or translation initiation with harringtonine almost entirely blocked the buildup of protein aggregates following 6 hr of bortezomib treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: When ISR-competent cells were treated with salubrinal, aberrant ubiquitinated aggregates accumulated following 24 hr of recovery from the bortezomib pulse.
source: Additionally, we found that the ability of a cell to resolve the ISR was required to promote clearance of protein aggregates. Thus, when ISR-competent cells were treated with salubrinal, a selective inhibitor of eIF2α dephosphorylation, aberrant ubiquitinated aggregates accumulated following 24 hr of recovery from the bortezomib pulse (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: BafA1 delayed recovery from proteotoxic stress partially but not fully, indicating that both autophagy and the proteasome cooperate in clearing ubiquitin-marked protein aggregates.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, BafA1 delayed recovery partially but not fully. Taken together, these data indicated that both autophagy and the proteasome cooperate in clearing these ubiquitin-marked protein aggregates during the recovery phase following proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: PERK participated in protein aggregate clearance independently of the ISR.
source: Indeed, inhibition of PERK signaling by GSK2606414 resulted in increased aggregate accumulation, but this appeared to be irrespective of the status of eIF2α. PERK participated in protein aggregate clearance independently of the ISR, suggesting that other PERK targets, possibly NRF2 (Pajares et al., 2017), may be involved.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and cited work from Pajares et al., 2017.

claim: 24 mRNAs surfaced as candidates for bona fide ISR translational targets and showed strong enrichment across all four sets of translational replicates of proteotoxic stress-induced SCC cells harboring an intact ISR.
source: By this criterion, 24 mRNAs surfaced as candidates for bona fide ISR translational targets and showed strong enrichment across all four sets of translational replicates of proteotoxic stress-induced SCC cells harboring an intact ISR (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The top three GO-terms for cellular components among ISR translational targets were centrosomal proteins, MTOC proteins, and microtubule cytoskeletal proteins.
source: Most intriguing, however, were the top three GO-terms for cellular components: centrosomal proteins, MTOC proteins, and microtubule cytoskeletal proteins (Figure 3G and genes highlighted in green in Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ATF5 mRNA displayed dramatic increases in translation in the absence of transcriptional upregulation and specifically in ISR-competent SCC cells exposed to proteotoxic stress.
source: Of further intrigue was the mRNA for ATF5, which, like that for ATF4, displayed dramatic increases in translation in the absence of transcriptional upregulation and specifically in ISR-competent SCC cells exposed to proteotoxic stress (Figure 3H and I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3H and I, and qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Fluorescence intensities of both pericentrin and γ-tubulin were significantly increased in control, but not ISR-null cells, specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress.
source: Fluorescence intensities of both markers were significantly increased in control, but not ISR-null cells, and specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress since no changes were observed in vehicle-treated cells or upon recovery from oxidative and ER stress (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: The overall size of the MTOC was enlarged specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress and only when the ISR was intact.
source: Quantifications further revealed that the overall size of the MTOC was enlarged specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress and only when the ISR was intact (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Enlargement of the MTOC was dependent on eIF2α dephosphorylation.
source: Additionally, enlargement of the MTOC was dependent on eIF2α dephosphorylation, suggesting that while ISR-dependent synthesis of cytoskeletal proteins occurs early on during stress response, cellular recovery requires resolution of the ISR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pre-oncogenic and fully transformed keratinocytes both significantly increased MTOC size during the recovery phase from proteotoxic stress, while keratinocytes isolated from littermate control mice failed to do so.
source: While pre-oncogenic and fully transformed keratinocytes both significantly increased MTOC size during the recovery phase from proteotoxic stress, keratinocytes isolated from littermate control mice failed to do so (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Microtubule growth from the MTOC was markedly impaired in ISR-null compared to control SCC cells after 4 hr of bortezomib recovery.
source: Even after 4 hr of bortezomib recovery, microtubule growth from the MTOC was still markedly impaired in the ISR-null compared to control SCC cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Live imaging revealed a significant delay in new microtubules nucleating from the centrosomes in S51A cells specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress.
source: Live imaging of S51 and S51A cells showed no overt differences in the microtubule cytoskeleton of unstressed cells. However, when combined with nocodazole recovery, SiR-tubulin imaging revealed a significant delay in new microtubules nucleating from the centrosomes in S51A cells specifically during recovery from proteotoxic stress (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures.

claim: Misfolded protein aggregates began to coalesce into the aggresome soon after bortezomib withdrawal in S51 cells, peaking at approximately 8 hr into the recovery phase.
source: As judged by convergence of intense anti-p62 immunofluorescence to a single large perinuclear spot within each S51 cell, misfolded protein aggregates began to coalesce into the aggresome soon after bortezomib withdrawal, peaking at approximately 8 hr into the recovery phase (Figure 5B, top panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only a few S51A cells displayed the bright perinuclear spot reflective of the aggresome at 8 hr after bortezomib withdrawal.
source: However, even at 8 hr after bortezomib withdrawal, only a few S51A cells displayed the bright perinuclear spot reflective of the aggresome.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Electron-dense protein aggregates pushing into the nucleus were observed in the perinuclear regions of S51 but not S51A SCC cells after 8 hr of recovery.
source: After 8 hr of recovery, electron-dense protein aggregates pushing into the nucleus were observed in the perinuclear regions of S51 but not S51A SCC cells.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Microtubule stabilization with paclitaxel potently blocked aggresome formation, phenocopying the ISR-null cells during this process.
source: In line with our hypothesis, microtubule stabilization with paclitaxel potently blocked aggresome formation, phenocopying the ISR-null cells during this process (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Upon proteotoxic stress the ISR promoted a remodeling in cell morphology evident by diminished focal adhesion and F-actin staining.
source: As judged by immunofluorescence for vinculin, upon proteotoxic stress the ISR promoted a remodeling in cell morphology evident by diminished focal adhesion and F-actin staining.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ISR-null SCC cells recovering from proteotoxic stress possessed large, stable focal adhesions that did not disassemble, rendering the cell immobile.
source: Indeed, ISR-null SCC cells recovering from proteotoxic stress possessed large, stable focal adhesions that did not disassemble, rendering the cell immobile over the time frame, whereas control SCC cells disassembled their large focal adhesions and displayed considerable dynamics (Figure 6B, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ISR-null cells showed markedly impaired mobility relative to control cells and failed to migrate into the wound site in a scratch wound assay following bortezomib treatment.
source: To confirm these aberrant dynamics, we performed a scratch wound assay to induce cell migration following bortezomib treatment. In agreement with our previous data showing large and stable focal adhesion, ISR-null cells showed markedly impaired mobility relative to control cells and failed to migrate into the wound site (Figure 6C, Figure 6—video 2, Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ATF5 is translated only during proteotoxic stress, in contrast to ATF4 that is broadly induced to stress.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to ATF4 that is broadly induced to stress, we found that ATF5 is translated only during proteotoxic stress (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Upon recovery from proteotoxic stress ATF5 localized at the centrosome in ISR-competent SCC cells.
source: In agreement with the notion that ATF5 may play a selective role in clearance of protein aggregates, confocal microscopy revealed that upon recovery from proteotoxic stress ATF5 localized at the centrosome in ISR-competent SCC cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of ATF5 significantly improved the ability of ISR-null cells to clear ubiquitinated proteins after 24 hr recovery from bortezomib.
source: Remarkably, expression of ATF5 significantly improved the ability of ISR-null cells to clear ubiquitinated proteins, as assessed by immunoblot of ubiquitinated proteins in the insoluble fraction of cells after 24 hr recovery from bortezomib (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: ATF5 expression corresponded with a significant increase in aggresome formation in ISR-null cells.
source: Strikingly, this corresponded with a significant increase in aggresome formation, indicating that ISR-mediated ATF5 upregulation is needed to promote the retrograde transport of misfolded proteins and the subsequent accumulation of protein aggregates at the MTOC (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: ATF5 expression increased pericentrin mean fluorescence intensity at the centrosome in ISR-null cells after recovery from bortezomib treatment.
source: This effect was mediated via protection of microtubule dynamics as evidenced by increased pericentrin mean fluorescence intensity at the centrosome in ISR-null cells expressing ATF5 after recovery from bortezomib treatment (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Short-hairpin-RNA-mediated ATF5 knockdown in ISR-competent cells resulted in higher accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and reduced aggresome formation during recovery from proteotoxic stress.
source: Strengthening this mechanistic link, short-hairpin-RNA-mediated ATF5 knockdown in ISR-competent cells resulted in higher accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and reduced aggresome formation during recovery from proteotoxic stress (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Control keratinocytes mounted an ISR in response to bortezomib but failed to induce Atf5 translation despite expressing similar levels of Atf5 mRNA compared to transformed cells.
source: In response to bortezomib, control keratinocytes mounted an ISR, as judged by eIF2α phosphorylation, and upregulated ATF4 although at lower level compared to transformed cells. Yet, despite expressing similar levels of Atf5 mRNA, untransformed cells failed to induce Atf5 translation and showed no ATF5 protein expression (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and qPCR data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ATF5 expression rescued the selective sensitivity to bortezomib shown by ISR-null cells in vivo.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, ATF5 expression rescued the selective sensitivity to bortezomib shown by ISR-null cells. This occurred in the absence of changes in viability in tumors at steady state (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The ISR is not only required to mount a stress response, but also to instruct cell function during recovery from stress.
source: Our findings led us to the remarkable conclusion that the ISR is not only required to mount a stress response, but also to instruct cell function during recovery from stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: When ISR-competent cells are exposed to proteotoxic stress, they redirect their translational machinery to a cohort of mRNAs encoding centrosomal proteins.
source: Specifically, we learned that when ISR-competent cells are exposed to proteotoxic stress, they redirect their translational machinery to a cohort of mRNAs encoding centrosomal proteins.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Centrosomal proteins function in bolstering the MTOC and reinforcing its microtubule dynamics to facilitate efficient microtubule-mediated transport of misfolded proteins to the perinuclear space.
source: We show that these proteins function in bolstering the MTOC and reinforcing its microtubule dynamics. This then facilitates efficient microtubule-mediated transport of misfolded proteins to the perinuclear space, where they can be assembled into aggresomes and targeted for ubiquitin-mediated degradation during the stress recovery phase.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental findings including MTOC enlargement, microtubule dynamics assays, and aggresome formation data.

claim: The ISR not only upregulates a subset of centrosomal proteins, but also downregulates focal adhesion components.
source: Compellingly, the ISR not only upregulates a subset of centrosomal proteins, but also downregulates focal adhesion components, surfacing a network of ISR-regulated cytoskeletal dynamics that directs morphological changes critical for cell recovery.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data showing downregulation of focal adhesion genes and immunofluorescence data showing changes in focal adhesion morphology.

claim: ISR-mediated translational upregulation of centrosomal proteins, including ATF5, is required to remodel the MTOC and concentrate protein aggregates in the perinuclear space.
source: Our data support a model in which ISR-mediated translational upregulation of centrosomal proteins, including ATF5, is required to remodel the MTOC and concentrate protein aggregates in the perinuclear space so that they can be degraded and cleared by proteosomes and autophagosomes.
evidence: This is a model supported by multiple experimental findings including ribosome profiling, MTOC enlargement, aggresome formation, and ATF5 rescue experiments.

claim: Atf5 translational upregulation is limited to proteotoxic stress and unique to transformed skin stem cells.
source: Our findings that Atf5 translational upregulation is limited to proteotoxic stress and unique to transformed skin stem cells is particularly intriguing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing ATF5 induction in control versus transformed keratinocytes shown in Figure 7H.
